_source.displaydescription:
There are only few examples of big caityas constructed in the center of a bāhāḥ courtyard.  Its shape closely resembles a Vajradhātu Caitya found in abundance in the Valley.

Statues of Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi are located in niches facing east, west, south, and north respectively. The caitya’s harmika, toraṇa, trayodaśabhuvana, and its pinnacle are covered with copper gilt. A yaṣṭhī is installed inside it. It is one of the oldest caityas in the Valley with its old yaṣṭhī remaining intact (Gutschow 1997, 24). Locals believe that there is an Aśoka Caitya inside the caitya’s garbha (H. Śākya NS 1099, 31).

There is scant inscriptive evidence to appoint caitya’s initial construction. H. Śākya writes that the caitya’s current look dates back to the nineteenth century. In 1868 CE (NS 989), an individual named Cikidhana Tāmrākāra renovated the caitya, and offered a gilt cakrāvalī and parasol at the top of the caitya.

During this renovation, the caitya’s yaṣṭhī was also replaced. A statue of Lokeśvara carved from the original yaṣṭhī is kept safe inside the caitya’s garbha (H. Śākya NS 1099, 46-46). It was also renovated in 1976 CE (VS 2035). In the present-day (in 2021 CE), the Federal Government is renovating residential buildings, the dyaḥchẽ, and caitya’s plinth.

A local Udāy Guṭhī organises the anniversary of the caitya on the full moon day of Asauja (Āśvina). Tutaḥ Guṭhī members recite strotras in front of the caitya during the entire month of Guṃlā as well as on other auspicious days.

_source.displaydescription:
This free-standing three-bay Phalcā faces east and is located in the north of Thati courtyard. Dabū Phalcā contains carved wooden pillars (dhaliṃkhvāḥ) and small windows which can be dated back to the 17th century. Six old columns with kalasa motifs, a capital showing a dragon, small windows and rare panels have been preserved. The Phalcā's roof is covered with jhĩgaṭī tiles and has been recently repaired by a Khaḍgī at his own cost. Inside, one can find two inscriptions and a statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara.

The chariot of Matsyendranātha stops at the Thati Ṭola for several days, where it rests in the public space between this and two other phalcās. One of the inscriptions in this Phalcā mentions that it was constructed in 1704 CE (NS 824) by Narahari Bhāro and his wife Vasumuni, residents of Dhopogatra (present Dhaugala ṭola) during the reign of Yoganarendra Malla. The same inscription mentions the construction of a stage platform (dabū), though this has since been removed. 

The second inscription states that Siddhivajra Vajrācārya from Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra recited Guṇakāraṇyavyūha at the chariot procession of Matsyendranātha in 1868 CE (NS 988). The inscription does not mention whether the recitation took place inside the Phalcā or somewhere else. The building was reconstructed one month after this recitation took place. A representative of each of the four major Vihāras of Patan was involved in both the recitation and the reconstruction process. No religious or cultural activities are observed here any longer.

_source.displaydescription:
Amṛta Hiti, locally known as Pvaḥ Hiti, was constructed during the medieval period for the Poḍhe community residing in Imūkhel, Lalitpur.

The hiti has two water conduits, facing east. Generally, statues of Bhagīratha are installed under the water spout(s) of a hiti, however, this is not the case in Amṛta Hiti. A statue of Śrīdhara Viṣṇu is established on the hiti’s northern wall which S. Khanal  (2068, 173) dates to the sixteenth and seventeenth century. The source of water for this hiti  originates from the hillock of Imūdvã. Due to rapid urbanization, the underground water level is depleting, hence the hiti dries up during winter and flows only during the monsoon season.

There is no evidence to appoint the initial construction of the hiti. However, it is probable that it was built sometime during the medieval period (Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City 2007, 45). It was renovated by the local community in 1988 CE (VS 2045). The UN-Habitat and Integrated Urban Development Project assisted to form a local committee in 2008 CE (VS 2065) for the management of water collection from the hiti during the night and distributing it to the public during the day. However, this plan did not work out.

The local community cleans the hiti on the day of the Sithinakhaḥ, the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.
